request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Age: 70 years old

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with worsening right upper quadrant pain, anorexia, and 10 lb weight loss. A CT scan revealed hepatomegaly and several hypodense lesions consistent with liver metastases, indicating recurrent/metastatic disease. The patient was started on pembrolizumab and axitinib as first-line therapy for her condition.

During treatment, the patient experienced side effects and required a dose reduction of axitinib due to fatigue. Elevated thyroid stimulating hormone levels were also monitored and subsequently managed with medication.

After 12 weeks of combination axitinib/pembrolizumab, repeat CT scans showed progression of liver metastases, prompting a liver biopsy.

Genomic testing revealed loss of function mutations in von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) and BRCA1-associated protein (BAP1) genes, as well as copy-number loss of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A).

The patient was discharged home with appropriate follow-up measures.
Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Procedures:
1. CT-guided liver biopsy

Updated Medications:
None.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will receive appropriate follow-up care as recommended by her healthcare provider.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: C64**

The summary doesn't name the primary site, but the picture points to metastatic renal cell carcinoma. VHL loss and BAP1 mutation are characteristic of clear cell RCC, and first-line pembrolizumab with axitinib is standard therapy for advanced RCC. The liver lesions (C78.7) are secondary deposits, and the episode was chiefly for investigating and treating the underlying malignancy, so the principal diagnosis is the primary kidney cancer, malignant neoplasm of kidney (C64).
